title: Beyond Continuity: Simulation-free Reconstruction of Discrete Branching Dynamics from Single-cell Snapshots
claim: A baseline yields noisy, inconsistent per-cluster growth estimates, while ours recovers clean, correct growth rates for each population.
layout: 2 side-by-side scatter panels, shared colorbar at right, same axes
description: Two side-by-side 2D scatter plots share the same axes (X1 horizontal, X2 vertical) and a vertical diverging colorbar on the right labeled 'Predicted growth rate', ranging from -2 (blue) to 2 (red). The left panel is titled WFR-FM and the right panel is titled USB. Each panel shows four Gaussian point clusters: one at the top (around X1=0, X2=2.5) and three along the bottom (X1=-1, 0, 1 at X2=0). In WFR-FM, the top cluster is a mix of red and orange points, and the bottom clusters are light blue, medium blue and orange, so the estimates are inconsistent and noisy. In USB, the top cluster is uniformly deep red and the bottom clusters are uniformly pale yellow, near zero growth. The eye goes first to the strong red cluster and the contrast in color uniformity.
caption: Learned growth rate on the Gaussian 1000D dataset. Left panel: WFR-FM; Right panel: USB
abstract: Inferring cellular trajectories from destructive snapshots is complicated by the challenges of stochasticity and non-conservative mass dynamics such as cell proliferation and apoptosis. Existing unbalanced Optimal Transport (OT) methods treat mass as a continuous fluid, performing inference at the population level. However, this macroscopic view often fails to capture the discrete, jump-like nature of birth-death events at single-cell resolution, which is essential for understanding lineage branching and fate decisions. We present Unbalanced SchrÃ¶dinger Bridge (USB), a simulation-free framework for learning underlying dynamics that effectively integrates both stochastic and unbalanced effects which also models the discrete, jump-like birth-death dynamics at single-cell resolution. Theoretically, USB provides a tractable solution to the Branching SchrÃ¶dinger Bridge (BSB) problem, offering a rigorous microscopic interpretation where individual cells undergo both Brownian motion and discrete birth-death jumps. Technically, the method implements an efficient solver by introducing a simulation-free training objective that effectively scales to high-dimensional omics data. Empirically, we demonstrate on both simulated and real-world datasets that USB not only achieves trajectory reconstruction performance better than or comparable to deterministic baselines but also uniquely enables realistic discrete simulation of birth-death dynamics at single-cell resolution.
